strengths: The core idea—contrastive learning between proprioceptive and privileged states (available via the common asymmetric actor-critic setup) to improve proprioceptive representations—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained with a SimSiam-style formulation and zero-masking to align dimensionality.

The paper contributes SRL4Humanoid, a modular open-source framework implementing multiple representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction-based VAE, dynamics-modeling SPR, contrastive SimSiam) alongside PvP, which could be a useful community resource for systematic study of SRL in humanoid RL.

Experimental evaluation is reasonably broad for a single-robot study: two distinct WBC tasks (velocity tracking and motion imitation), four baseline comparisons, and six targeted ablations/analyses (training-time proportion, training-data proportion, which encoder benefits from SRL, computational overhead, and Sim2Sim/real-robot validation).

Practical, non-obvious findings are reported, such as SRL applied to the value encoder causing training collapse in the velocity task, and the need for an interval-update mechanism to prevent premature convergence to local optima — these provide actionable guidance beyond just the headline result.
The approach is validated beyond simulation with Sim2Sim (MuJoCo) and real hardware deployment on the LimX Oli humanoid, which is more convincing than simulation-only evaluation.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single robot platform (LimX Oli) and only two tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation); no manipulation or more diverse terrain/task settings are tested despite the paper's broader WBC framing, limiting evidence for generality.

The comparison against baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) may not isolate the actual source of PvP's gains: baselines only use proprioceptive-only contrastive/reconstruction objectives, while PvP additionally exploits privileged information. A control baseline that simply concatenates or predicts privileged features into the encoder without contrastive structure (or that gives baselines access to the same privileged signal) is missing, making it hard to attribute improvement specifically to the contrastive mechanism rather than to added information access.

Real-world evaluation (Section 5.2.6, Figure 1c/11) is qualitative only (image sequences), without quantitative real-robot metrics (e.g., tracking error, energy consumption, failure rate), weakening claims of "reliable real-world deployment."

No comparison to strong non-SRL, task-specific humanoid WBC baselines (e.g., the cited BeyondMimic, HugWBC) is provided to contextualize whether PvP-enhanced PPO is competitive with state-of-the-art absolute performance, only relative gains over an internal PPO baseline are shown.

The number of random seeds used to generate the shown mean/std shaded regions is not explicitly stated, and no significance testing is reported, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported improvements.

Minor clarity issues: some figures (e.g., Fig. 2) have small/unclear labels ("Poicy Encoder"), and detailed justification for specific design choices (e.g., why root linear velocity/orientation specifically chosen as privileged targets, why interval of 50 is optimal) is largely empirical/ad hoc rather than principled.

strengths: Proposes a simple, well-motivated contrastive learning approach (PvP) that exploits complementary information between proprioceptive and privileged states, avoiding hand-crafted data augmentations that are typically needed by contrastive SRL methods.

Introduces SRL4Humanoid, a unified, modular open-source benchmarking framework for systematically comparing SRL methods (reconstruction-based VAE, dynamics-modeling SPR, contrastive SimSiam) in humanoid WBC RL, which could be a useful community resource for reproducible research.

Extensive empirical study addressing multiple practical research questions (update interval, training data proportion, which encoder to apply SRL to, computational overhead), going beyond a single headline result to provide actionable design guidance.

Evaluation spans two distinct benchmark tasks (velocity tracking and motion imitation) plus appendix experiments on additional terrain and a different robot platform (Unitree G1), as well as real-world hardware deployment and Sim2Sim validation on MuJoCo, which strengthens claims about the practical usefulness of the method.

Comparison against teacher-student distillation (TSD) baselines in the appendix, clarifying PvP's conceptual advantage of jointly evolving representation and policy rather than relying on a fixed pretrained teacher.

Ablation on the loss weighting coefficient and on applying SRL loss to policy vs. value encoder provides useful mechanistic insight (e.g., collapse observed when applying SRL to value encoder in velocity task).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental: it is essentially SimSiam contrastive learning applied to a privileged/proprioceptive pair with zero-masking, closely resembling existing contrastive-privileged-information approaches (e.g., PIM) with an added second modality; the novelty relative to combining known asymmetric actor-critic and contrastive SSL ideas is limited and could be more clearly delineated from prior work such as PIM and teacher-student distillation.

Real-robot evaluation (Q6, Figure 1c) is only qualitatively illustrated with a handful of frames and referenced supplementary videos, without any quantitative real-world metrics (e.g., tracking error, success rate, robustness under disturbance), limiting the strength of claims about real-world deployment reliability.

All main experiments are conducted on a single primary robot (LimX Oli) with only two tasks; while appendix adds a second robot (Unitree G1) and a rough-terrain variant, the number of seeds/runs is not clearly reported and statistical significance of differences (e.g., error bars appear as shaded std across few seeds) is not rigorously established.

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6, indicator function to update SRL loss every T steps) is introduced somewhat ad hoc based on an informally described training collapse observation, without a systematic ablation showing how T was selected and how sensitive results are to it beyond Figure 8's coarse sweep.

Baseline hyperparameter tuning appears limited to a coarse grid search (e.g., {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}) for each baseline SRL method, raising some concern that baselines (VAE, SPR) might be under-tuned relative to the proposed method, which could inflate the apparent gap.

The paper's claimed generality ("highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of tasks") is only tested on WBC-style locomotion/imitation; no manipulation or more complex embodied tasks are evaluated despite motivating the work with manipulation and dynamic-environment interaction.

Presentation clarity could be improved: some figures (e.g., Figure 9, 10) have small/dense subplots that are hard to parse, and the interval-update mechanism explanation in the main text is somewhat terse relative to its apparent empirical importance.
